subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before an appointment is made.
summary: Mariposa does the hardest thing well. Kristy Murrow is named on the homepage as managing partner with her qualification — P.A.-C — and her specific certifications in Botox, dermal fillers, laser, sclerotherapy and PRP. Named patient reviews follow. Most practices we review never answer the question “who is holding the needle”, and this one answers it plainly.

The opportunity is on the first screen. The practice's own name appears three times before a visitor sees anything else — once in the logo, once as a full-width headline in capitals, and once again in “Welcome to Mariposa Aesthetics & Laser Center”. The only two buttons offered read “View Specials” and “Shop Products”. Neither books an appointment, and no telephone number appears until the visitor scrolls.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The trust work here is already done and done well — most of what follows is about what the first screen asks the visitor to do.

scorecard.finding: The practice name appears three times before anything else does.
Practitioner named with real credentials — but not until the visitor scrolls.
The two hero buttons sell specials and products, not appointments.
Two competing actions, neither of which is the one that earns.
Clean and readable, but no booking or tap-to-call on the first screen.
Phone and Classen Blvd address present and consistent.

strengthsLead: The first two of these are the hardest things on any aesthetic site to get right, and they are already right here.

strengths.title: The practitioner is named, with real credentials.
strengths.body: Kristy Murrow, P.A.-C, identified as managing partner, with certifications listed in Botox, dermal fillers, laser treatments, sclerotherapy and PRP. This is the single most valuable trust signal an aesthetic practice can publish, and most do not.

strengths.title: Patient reviews carry real names.
strengths.body: A “Patient Reviews” section with named reviewers and treatment-specific comments. Named, specific reviews are read as credible in a way that anonymous five-star blocks are not.

strengths.title: Retail is already part of the business.
strengths.body: “Shop Products” indicates product sales are set up. Retail earns margin without consuming a room or a practitioner's hour, and a great many practices never build the path at all.

strengths.title: The mobile page is clean and legible.
strengths.body: Generous type, clear buttons, no clutter fighting the message. Nothing here needs rebuilding — the elements simply need reordering.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The practice name appears in the logo and again as the headline. The two visible buttons are “View Specials” and “Shop Products”.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. Same pattern, with “Welcome to Mariposa Aesthetics & Laser Center” following immediately below — the name a third time.

findings.heading: Neither button on the first screen books an appointment.
findings.evidence: The two buttons in the hero read “View Specials” and “Shop Products”. The instruction “Call now to make an appointment” appears further down the page. No telephone number is visible on the first screen on either desktop or mobile.
findings.why: The visitor most worth catching is the one who has already decided. They are offered a discount page and a shop, and have to scroll to find out how to actually be seen. Meanwhile “View Specials” invites a price-led visitor — the opposite of the full-fee patient the credentials on this site are built to attract.
findings.recommended: Make “Book an Appointment” the primary button, with the telephone number beside it as a tap-to-call link. Keep Specials and Shop as secondary links — they are good, they are simply in the wrong position in the queue.

findings.heading: The practice name appears three times before anything else does.
findings.evidence: “Mariposa Aesthetics & Laser Center” appears in the logo, again as a full-width headline set in capitals across the hero photograph, and a third time in the “Welcome to Mariposa Aesthetics & Laser Center” heading immediately below.
findings.why: Everyone reading it arrived by clicking the practice's name, so all three repetitions tell them nothing new. The most valuable space on the site is spent confirming something already known, in place of what the practice does, who it suits, and why choose it.
findings.recommended: Let the logo carry the name. Give the headline to the offer and the city — the sort of line a patient could repeat to a friend — and change “Welcome to…” to something that moves the visitor forward.

findings.heading: “Superior service comes standard” is a claim the visitor cannot check.
findings.evidence: The supporting line reads “At Mariposa Aesthetics & Laser Center, superior service comes standard!”
findings.why: Every competitor says a version of this, so it distinguishes nothing — and a sceptical first-time patient discounts claims a practice makes about itself. The evidence that would persuade them is already on this site, further down: a named P.A.-C with listed certifications, and reviews from named patients.
findings.recommended: Replace the claim with the proof. A line naming the practitioner and her qualification does more in ten words than any superlative, and it is already true.

findings.heading: The best asset on the site is below the decision.
findings.evidence: Kristy Murrow's name, qualification and certifications appear on the homepage, but below the hero. No credential and no review appear on the first screen.
findings.why: Proof only works where doubt happens. A visitor deciding whether this practice is serious has to scroll past that decision to find the evidence that would have settled it.
findings.recommended: Lift the practitioner's name, qualification and photograph into the hero, and place one short patient quote beside the booking button. Nothing new needs writing — it needs moving.

findings.heading: Every appointment has to become a phone call.
findings.evidence: No online booking or enquiry form was found from the homepage. The route to an appointment is “Call now to make an appointment”.
findings.why: A large share of aesthetic research happens in the evening, when nobody is answering. Phone-only means the practice competes only during office hours, against clinics that accept a booking at eleven at night with nobody present.
findings.recommended: Add a booking path that completes on your own site. Even a short enquiry form capturing name, treatment of interest and preferred time will catch the patient who will not telephone a stranger.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Layout and menu follow convention well; nothing here surprises a visitor.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Both hero buttons are generous, well-placed tap targets. The mechanics are right; the destinations are wrong.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: Credentials and named reviews exist, but all of them sit below the first screen.
Strong on the page overall — Kristy Murrow, P.A.-C with listed certifications — but absent from the opening screen.
Two buttons of equal weight, neither of which is booking. The patient must decide what the practice wants.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Leading with “Specials” sets a price frame before value has been established, which works against the full-fee patient.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “Superior service comes standard” is the least believable line on a page that is otherwise well evidenced.

roadmap.actions: Make “Book an Appointment” the primary hero button with a tap-to-call number beside it. Demote Specials and Shop to secondary links. Replace the headline with the offer and the city rather than the practice name.
Lift Kristy Murrow's name, qualification and photograph into the hero. Place one patient quote beside the booking button. Replace “superior service comes standard” with the credential that proves it.

Add an online booking or enquiry path that completes on your own site. Treatment-page depth with realistic expectations. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
